chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
stem: Bones contain ____ amino acids.
solution: Ossein is the protein (made of amino acids) found in bones; it forms the organic matrix on which the mineral salts of bone are deposited. Melanin and keratin are the proteins of skin, haemoglobin is the protein of blood (RBCs) and insulin is the protein hormone secreted by the pancreas. Hence the correct alternative is (C) Ossein.

stem: Giant squirrel is an example of ____ threatened species.
solution: Indeterminate species are those species which are known to be threatened (extinct, endangered, vulnerable or rare) but about which there is not enough information — because of their shy or secretive habits and restricted habitat — to decide which of those categories they actually belong to. The Giant squirrel (Shekru, the State animal of Maharashtra) is the textbook example of an indeterminate threatened species. Hence the correct alternative is (D) Indeterminate.

stem: Human being belongs to ____ class.
solution: Human beings have hair on the body, mammary glands that secrete milk to feed the young, a four-chambered heart, a muscular diaphragm, external ears (pinnae) and they give birth to young ones (viviparous). All these are characters of class Mammalia. Hence the correct alternative is (A) Mammalia.

stem: Organs like ____ can be donated after death.
solution: Organ donation means giving one's organs after death for transplantation into a needy patient. Vital ORGANS such as the heart, kidneys, liver, lungs and pancreas are retrieved and donated after (brain) death, whereas skin and bones are donated as TISSUES rather than as organs. The heart is the standard textbook example of an organ that can be donated after death. Hence the correct alternative is (B) Heart. [Note: lungs (option C) is also an organ that can be donated after brain death, so the question does not discriminate perfectly; the published key is (B).]

stem: Volcano is a ____ disaster.
solution: A volcanic eruption is caused by movements and processes taking place inside the crust of the earth, i.e. by geological changes. Therefore, along with earthquakes, landslides and tsunamis, a volcano is classified as a geological (natural) disaster. Hence the correct alternative is (D) Geological.

stem:
Find the odd one out:
Earthquake, Flooding, Tsunami, War
solution:
Odd one out: War.
Earthquake, flooding and tsunami are natural disasters caused by natural processes, whereas war is a man-made (human-induced) disaster.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
stem:
State true or false:
Oxidation of proteins is carried out in aerobic respiration.
solution:
False.
In aerobic respiration it is the carbohydrate glucose \(\left( \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 \right)\) that is completely oxidised in the presence of oxygen to give carbon dioxide, water and energy (ATP). Glucose is the normal respiratory substrate; proteins are body-building nutrients and are not the substance oxidised in aerobic respiration. Hence the statement is false.

solution:

Just as the Asiatic lion is the characteristic protected animal associated with the given region, the Royal Bengal tiger is the characteristic protected animal of the Sunderban (mangrove) sanctuary/biosphere reserve.

stem: Which type of fuel is used in thermal power plant?
solution: Fossil fuel — mainly coal — is used in a thermal power plant. Coal is burnt to boil water and produce high pressure steam, which rotates the turbine coupled to the generator. (Natural gas and petroleum products such as furnace oil are also used as fuel in some thermal power stations.)

solution: The picture shows a group of people standing together in a garden with their arms raised, laughing loudly together. It is a LAUGHTER CLUB (laughter therapy / laughing yoga session). Laughter therapy is a simple and effective remedy for relieving mental stress: hearty laughter improves breathing and blood circulation, releases tension and helps to maintain good mental and social health.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
stem: Give scientific reason: Cell division is one of the important properties of cell and organisms.
solution:
Cell division is the process by which a parent cell divides to form new daughter cells. It is important because:
1. Growth and development: a multicellular organism grows from a single fertilised egg into a complete body only because of repeated mitotic cell divisions.
2. Repair and replacement: dead, damaged and worn-out cells (skin cells, blood cells, cells of the inner lining of the intestine) are continuously replaced by new cells formed by mitosis, and wounds heal by cell division.
3. Reproduction: unicellular organisms such as Amoeba multiply directly by cell division, and many multicellular organisms reproduce asexually by budding, fragmentation and regeneration, all of which depend on cell division.
4. Formation of gametes and constancy of chromosome number: gametes are produced by meiosis, which halves the chromosome number so that the chromosome number of the species remains constant generation after generation, and the crossing over during meiosis produces variations.
Since the very existence, growth, repair and continuity of life depend on it, cell division is one of the most important properties of a cell and of organisms.

stem: Give scientific reason: Cockroach belongs to phylum Arthropoda.
solution:
The cockroach shows all the characteristic features of phylum Arthropoda:
1. Its body is covered with a hard exoskeleton made of chitin, which is shed periodically (moulting).
2. Its body is bilaterally symmetrical, triploblastic, segmented and divided into head, thorax and abdomen.
3. It bears jointed appendages — three pairs of jointed legs and two pairs of wings on the thorax and jointed antennae on the head. (Arthropoda literally means 'jointed legs'.)
4. It has an open type of circulatory system with a dorsal heart and colourless blood (haemolymph), respiration through tracheae, and a pair of compound eyes.
Because it possesses these arthropod characters, the cockroach is placed in phylum Arthropoda.

stem: Give scientific reason: Power generation plant based on natural gas is eco-friendly.
solution:
Natural gas is mainly methane \(\left( \text{CH}_4 \right)\) and it burns almost completely. Therefore, compared with a coal-based thermal power plant:
1. It produces far less carbon dioxide per unit of electricity, and almost no sulphur dioxide or oxides of nitrogen, so acid rain and air pollution are greatly reduced.
2. It produces practically no ash, soot or suspended particulate matter, so there is no problem of ash disposal and no dust pollution.
3. Gas turbine (combined cycle) plants have a higher efficiency, so less fuel is burnt for the same amount of electricity.
4. Natural gas is transported by pipeline, so there is no pollution caused by transport and storage of solid fuel.
Hence a power generation plant based on natural gas is comparatively eco-friendly.

stem: Complete the following diagram (chart of 'Evidences of Evolution' — two boxes, 'Morphological' and 'Similarities in bone structure', are given and four boxes are blank).
solution:
Completed chart — Evidences of Evolution:
1. Morphological evidences (given) — similarities in the external form and structure of related organisms.
2. Similarities in bone structure, i.e. anatomical evidences (given) — homologous organs such as the forelimbs of man, whale, bat and horse have the same bone plan.
3. Palaeontological evidences (fossils) — remains and impressions of extinct organisms preserved in rocks show the gradual changes that occurred over time.
4. Vestigial organs — functionless remnants such as the vermiform appendix, nictitating membrane, ear muscles and tail bone (coccyx) in man.
5. Connecting links — organisms such as Peripatus (between Annelida and Arthropoda), lung fish and Duckbill platypus that show characters of two different groups.
6. Embryological evidences — early embryos of fish, tortoise, bird and man look remarkably similar, indicating a common ancestry. (Biochemical/genetic evidences — similarities in proteins, DNA and blood — are also accepted.)
figureNote: Chart/concept map: central shaded box 'Evidences of Evolution' with six arrows to six boxes — 'Morphological' (top-left) and 'Similarities in bone structure' (bottom-left) are printed, the other four boxes are blank and are to be filled, p-01.

stem: What do we learn from the story of Jadav Molai Payeng?
solution:
Jadav Molai Payeng of Assam, known as the 'Forest Man of India', began planting saplings on a barren, eroded sandbar of the river Brahmaputra when he was a teenager and continued patiently for several decades, single-handedly raising a dense forest of about 550 hectares (the 'Molai forest') which is today home to elephants, rhinoceros, deer, tigers and many birds.
What we learn from his story:
1. Even one determined and persevering individual can bring about a huge change in the environment — no effort at conservation is too small.
2. Regular, patient and continuous work is more valuable than a single big effort.
3. Afforestation restores degraded land, prevents soil erosion and recreates the habitat of wildlife, thereby restoring ecological balance.
4. Protecting nature is everyone's personal responsibility, not only the Government's; each of us should plant and nurture trees.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
stem: Distinguish between sexual reproduction and asexual reproduction. (two points)
solution:
| Sexual reproduction | Asexual reproduction |
|---|---|
| Two parents (male and female) are usually needed. | Only a single parent is needed. |
| Gametes are formed by meiosis and male and female gametes fuse (fertilisation) to form a zygote. | No gametes are formed and there is no fertilisation; the new organism is formed by mitotic division of body cells. |
| The offspring are not identical to the parents; variations arise, which are useful for evolution. | The offspring are exact copies (clones) of the parent; variations are almost absent. |
| It is a slow process. | It is a rapid process. |
| Examples: human beings, flowering plants. | Examples: Amoeba (binary fission), yeast (budding), Spirogyra (fragmentation), Planaria (regeneration). |

stem: Define genetically modified crops and give any two examples.
solution:
Definition: Genetically modified (GM) crops are those crop plants whose genetic material (DNA) has been deliberately altered by inserting a desired gene taken from another organism by the techniques of genetic engineering, so that the crop acquires a useful new character such as resistance to pests or diseases, tolerance to drought or herbicides, longer shelf life, higher yield or better nutritive value.
Examples (any two): (1) Bt cotton — carries a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis which makes it resistant to bollworm. (2) Golden rice — enriched with beta-carotene (provitamin A). (Other examples: Bt brinjal, Flavr Savr tomato with a longer shelf life.)

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 1
stem: What are vitamins? Write two types of vitamins.
solution:
Vitamins are organic compounds required by the body in very small (micro) quantities for the proper regulation of metabolism, for normal growth and for keeping the body healthy. They do not supply energy and are mostly not synthesised in the body, so they must be obtained through the diet; their deficiency causes deficiency diseases.
Two types of vitamins:
1. Fat-soluble vitamins — vitamins A, D, E and K. They dissolve in fats, can be stored in the body (liver and fatty tissue).
2. Water-soluble vitamins — vitamin C and the vitamin B-complex group. They dissolve in water, are not stored in the body and so must be supplied regularly in the diet.

stem: Explain the meanings of the following symbols: (1), (2) and (3).
solution:
(1) The symbol of a person dropping waste into a dustbin means: 'Do not litter — throw all waste only into a dustbin.' It stands for cleanliness and proper disposal/management of waste, which keeps the surroundings hygienic and prevents pollution and the spread of disease.
(2) The symbol of a bicycle means: 'Save fuel — use a bicycle instead of a motor vehicle for short distances.' Cycling does not consume petrol or diesel, so it conserves our limited fossil fuels, causes no air or noise pollution and also keeps the body fit.
(3) The symbol of two hands holding a drop means: 'Save water.' Water is a limited natural resource, so it must be used carefully, wastage must be avoided and rain water should be harvested and reused.
figureNote: Three pictorial symbols printed side by side under Q.3(i): (1) a circular badge showing a human figure putting a piece of waste into a dustbin, (2) a bicycle, (3) a pair of cupped hands holding a large drop, p-01.

stem: Write any three characteristics of class Reptilia.
solution:
Characteristics of class Reptilia (any three):
1. The body is covered with a dry, cornified skin bearing horny epidermal scales or scutes; skin glands are absent.
2. They are cold-blooded (poikilothermic) animals and creep or crawl on the ground; the limbs, when present, are two pairs, each usually with five clawed digits.
3. Respiration takes place only through lungs at every stage of life.
4. The heart is three-chambered (incompletely four-chambered in the crocodile).
5. They are oviparous — fertilisation is internal and they lay large, yolk-filled eggs covered with a leathery shell, usually on land.
6. Examples: lizard, snake, turtle, crocodile, chameleon.

context: Questions on the microbial production of cheese.
stem: Which substance is used to produce cheese?
solution: Milk (cow's or buffalo's milk) is the substance used to produce cheese. The milk is curdled with the help of lactic acid bacteria (Lactobacillus) and a milk-clotting enzyme; the curdled protein (casein) is then separated, pressed and ripened to form cheese.

context: Questions on the microbial production of cheese.
stem: Which enzyme was used earlier for cheese production?
solution: Earlier the enzyme RENNET (rennin, also called chymosin) was used. It was obtained from the inner lining of the stomach of a calf (a young, milk-fed animal), so cheese made with it was not suitable for vegetarians.

context: Questions on the microbial production of cheese.
stem: Which enzyme is used to produce vegetarian cheese?
solution: The enzyme PROTEASE, obtained from micro-organisms (microbial protease / microbially produced chymosin from fungi and genetically engineered bacteria), is used to produce vegetarian cheese. As it is not obtained from any animal, the cheese so produced is acceptable to vegetarians.

context: Refer to the diagram showing a single unspecialised cell which, on division, gives rise on one branch to identical copies of itself and on the other branch to several different specialised cells (a block of epithelial/muscle cells, red blood cells, a muscle fibre, a nerve cell and liver-type cells).
stem: Which process is shown in the given diagram?
solution: The diagram shows STEM CELLS and the process of their differentiation, i.e. stem cell therapy (stem cell culture). A stem cell is an undifferentiated cell which divides to form more stem cells (self-renewal) and can also differentiate into various types of specialised cells such as blood cells, muscle cells, nerve cells and liver cells.
figureNote: Diagram of a stem cell dividing: one arrow branch leads to two identical stem cells (self-renewal) and another branch leads to differentiated cells — a block of cuboidal cells, red blood cells, a muscle fibre, a nerve cell and a group of liver-like cells, p-01.

context: Refer to the diagram showing a single unspecialised cell which, on division, gives rise on one branch to identical copies of itself and on the other branch to several different specialised cells (a block of epithelial/muscle cells, red blood cells, a muscle fibre, a nerve cell and liver-type cells).
stem: What is the importance of this process?
solution:
Importance of stem cells and stem cell therapy:
1. Stem cells can divide continuously and can differentiate into any required type of cell, so they can regenerate and repair damaged or dead tissue.
2. They are used to treat diseases and disorders such as leukaemia and other blood disorders (by bone marrow transplantation), severe burns and skin injuries, damaged cornea, diabetes, Parkinson's disease, spinal-cord injury and heart-muscle damage.
3. Tissues and even whole organs can be grown from stem cells for transplantation, which reduces the shortage of donor organs and the risk of rejection when the patient's own stem cells are used.
4. Stem cells (for example from the umbilical cord blood at birth) can be preserved in stem-cell banks for future treatment, and they are also used in research on drugs and on human development.

context: Refer to the diagram showing a single unspecialised cell which, on division, gives rise on one branch to identical copies of itself and on the other branch to several different specialised cells (a block of epithelial/muscle cells, red blood cells, a muscle fibre, a nerve cell and liver-type cells).
stem: Which organs can be transplanted by this process?
solution: Tissues and organs that can be regenerated or transplanted with the help of stem cells include: bone marrow (blood-forming tissue), skin, cornea of the eye, and organs such as the kidney, liver, heart and pancreas; damaged nerve tissue, cartilage and bone can also be repaired. Bone-marrow (stem-cell) transplantation for blood disorders and skin grafting for burns are the treatments most commonly carried out today.

stem: What is meant by disaster? Write any two examples of each natural and man-made disaster.
solution:
Disaster: A disaster is a sudden, unexpected and serious event or calamity which disturbs the normal functioning of society and causes widespread loss of human and animal life, damage to property, and destruction of natural resources and the environment, to an extent that the affected community cannot cope with it using its own resources.
Natural disasters (any two): earthquake, flood, cyclone, tsunami, landslide, volcanic eruption, drought.
Man-made disasters (any two): war, terrorist attack, industrial or chemical gas leak (for example the Bhopal gas tragedy), fire, road/rail/air accidents, nuclear accidents, building collapse.

stem: Write the objections raised against Darwin's theory of natural selection.
solution:
Objections raised against Darwin's theory of natural selection:
1. Darwin could explain the survival of the fittest but could not explain the ORIGIN of variations — he did not know how or why variations arise.
2. He did not distinguish between somatic (acquired, non-heritable) variations and germinal (heritable) variations, and treated all variations as inheritable.
3. He had no knowledge of the laws of heredity (Mendel's work) or of genes, chromosomes and mutations, so he could not explain how variations are transmitted to the next generation.
4. He gave importance only to small, continuous and gradual variations; he could not explain the sudden, large, discontinuous variations (mutations) which are now known to be important in evolution.
5. He could not explain how the small initial stages of a useful organ (incipient or rudimentary organs) survive when they are still too undeveloped to be of any advantage.
6. His theory does not satisfactorily explain the persistence of vestigial organs, over-specialisation of some organs (like the huge antlers of the extinct Irish elk) or the degeneration of organs.

context: Refer to the cyclic picture showing: 'Solar energy + \(\text{CO}_2\)' absorbed by trees (Biomass), then Harvesting, Threshing, Cellulose, 'Conversion of cellulose to glucose', Sugars, 'Liquid fuel production through fermentation', Biofuel used in a car, a truck and an aeroplane, each releasing \(\text{CO}_2\) which returns to the plants.
stem: Which process is shown in the above given picture?
solution: The picture shows the process of PRODUCTION OF BIOFUEL FROM BIOMASS — the biofuel (bio-energy) cycle. Green plants use solar energy and carbon dioxide to build biomass; the harvested and threshed biomass yields cellulose, which is converted into glucose (sugars) and then fermented to give a liquid biofuel. When this biofuel is burnt in vehicles the carbon dioxide released is again absorbed by the plants, so the cycle is complete and biofuel is a renewable, carbon-neutral source of energy.
figureNote: Large cyclic illustration of biofuel production from biomass, labelled 'Solar energy + CO2', 'Biomass', 'Harvesting', 'Threshing', 'Cellulose', 'Conversion of cellulose to glucose', 'Sugars', 'Liquid fuel production through fermentation', 'Biofuel', with a car, truck and aeroplane emitting CO2 back into the cycle, top of p-02.

context: Refer to the cyclic picture showing: 'Solar energy + \(\text{CO}_2\)' absorbed by trees (Biomass), then Harvesting, Threshing, Cellulose, 'Conversion of cellulose to glucose', Sugars, 'Liquid fuel production through fermentation', Biofuel used in a car, a truck and an aeroplane, each releasing \(\text{CO}_2\) which returns to the plants.
stem: Give two examples for liquid fuels and solid fuels obtained by this process.
solution:
Liquid fuels obtained from biomass (any two): (1) Bio-ethanol (alcohol) obtained by fermentation of sugars from sugarcane molasses, maize or other plant material. (2) Bio-diesel obtained from vegetable oils and oil-bearing seeds (for example jatropha, karanj).
Solid fuels obtained from biomass (any two): (1) Firewood (wood) and charcoal. (2) Dried cow-dung cakes; briquettes made from pressed agricultural waste such as bagasse and husk are also used.
figureNote: Same biofuel-from-biomass cyclic illustration, top of p-02.

stem: Complete the stages in electric generator using wind energy (a flow chart of four boxes joined by arrows).
solution:
Completed flow chart of an electric generator working on wind energy:
Wind energy (kinetic energy of moving air) \(\rightarrow\) Rotation of the blades of the wind mill (kinetic/mechanical energy) \(\rightarrow\) Rotation of the shaft of the generator (mechanical energy) \(\rightarrow\) Electrical energy (electricity).
Thus the kinetic energy of the wind turns the blades of the wind mill; the rotating blades turn the shaft of the generator through a gear box, and the generator converts this mechanical energy into electrical energy.
figureNote: Flow chart of four EMPTY rectangular boxes joined by three arrows (no labels printed), to be filled by the student, middle of p-02.

context: Printed on the paper as sub-question 'vi.' of Q.3, but 'vi.' has already been used earlier in Q.3 (Darwin's theory), so this is the eighth sub-question of Q.3 — a printing/numbering error in the source paper.
stem: Write limitations in an electric generator using wind energy.
solution:
Limitations of an electric generator using wind energy:
1. A wind mill works only where the wind speed is high and fairly steady (about 15 km/h or more), so only a few coastal and hilly sites are suitable.
2. Wind is not available uniformly throughout the day and the year, so electricity generation is irregular and a storage (battery) or a back-up supply is essential.
3. A single wind mill generates very little power, so a large number of wind mills (a wind farm) and hence a very large area of land are needed.
4. The initial cost of setting up a wind farm and the cost of maintenance are very high; the tower and blades must withstand storms, rain and the sun.
5. The rotating blades create noise pollution and are harmful to birds and bats.

stem: Sketch and label the essential and accessory whorls of flower.
solution:
A typical complete flower has four whorls arranged on the thalamus:
Accessory (non-essential) whorls — they protect the flower and attract pollinating agents, but do not take part directly in reproduction:
1. Calyx — the outermost whorl of green leaf-like SEPALS; it protects the flower in the bud stage.
2. Corolla — the whorl of brightly coloured PETALS; it attracts insects and birds for pollination.
Essential whorls — they produce the gametes and take direct part in reproduction:
3. Androecium — the male whorl, made of STAMENS. Each stamen has a filament (stalk) and an anther which produces pollen grains (male gametes).
4. Gynoecium (pistil/carpel) — the female whorl. Each carpel has a stigma (which receives pollen), a style (a tube) and a swollen ovary containing ovules (female gametes).
Labelled sketch (to be drawn): a vertical section of a flower showing, from outside inwards — pedicel, thalamus, sepal (calyx), petal (corolla), stamen with filament and anther (androecium), and pistil with stigma, style, ovary and ovule (gynoecium); label the calyx and corolla as the accessory whorls and the androecium and gynoecium as the essential whorls.

chapter: Life Processes in Living Organisms Part 2
context: Q.4 carries an internal choice — the candidate answers any ONE of Q.4(i) or Q.4(ii).
stem: What is pollination?
solution:
Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther of the stamen (male reproductive organ) to the stigma of the pistil (female reproductive organ) of a flower of the same species. It is the essential step that precedes fertilisation in flowering plants.
It is of two types: (1) Self-pollination — pollen is transferred to the stigma of the same flower or of another flower on the same plant; (2) Cross-pollination — pollen is carried to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species.

stem: Give any two examples of agents of pollination.
solution: Agents of pollination (any two): (1) Insects such as honey bees and butterflies (entomophily). (2) Wind (anemophily). Other agents are water (hydrophily) and animals such as birds and bats (ornithophily/chiropterophily).

context: 'What will you do?' — five situations, each to be answered with the action you would take. Q.4 carries an internal choice: the candidate answers any ONE of Q.4(i) or Q.4(ii).
stem: What will you do? You are spending more time on internet.
solution: I will realise that excessive use of the internet is a kind of addiction which wastes time, harms my eyes, posture and sleep, and cuts me off from family and friends. Therefore I will: fix a definite, limited time for using the internet and use it only for study and useful information; switch off data/notifications while studying and keep the mobile out of the bedroom at night; prepare a daily timetable giving time to studies, outdoor games, exercise, hobbies like reading or music, and to talking with family and friends; and if I still find it difficult to control, I will discuss it openly with my parents or teacher and take their help.

context: 'What will you do?' — five situations, each to be answered with the action you would take. Q.4 carries an internal choice: the candidate answers any ONE of Q.4(i) or Q.4(ii).
stem: What will you do? Child of your neighbour is addicted to tobacco chewing.
solution: I will befriend the child and, without scolding or insulting him, explain the harmful effects of tobacco — that it contains nicotine which causes addiction, and that tobacco chewing causes bad breath, stained teeth, mouth ulcers, loss of appetite and finally cancer of the mouth and throat. I will show him pictures and information about these effects and about people who suffered. I will inform his parents and, with them, take him to a doctor or a de-addiction centre for counselling and treatment. I will also help him keep away from the company that gave him the habit, encourage him to join games and other activities to divert his mind, and praise and support him for every step he takes to give it up.

context: 'What will you do?' — five situations, each to be answered with the action you would take. Q.4 carries an internal choice: the candidate answers any ONE of Q.4(i) or Q.4(ii).
stem: What will you do? Your sister has become incommunicative.
solution: Becoming silent and withdrawn is often a sign of stress, fear, depression or some trouble that the person is unable to share. I will therefore spend more time with my sister, talk to her gently and patiently and listen to her without criticising or making fun of her, so that she feels safe enough to open up. I will involve her in family activities, games, music, exercise and outings to lift her mood, and assure her of my support. I will inform my parents about the change in her behaviour, and if she remains withdrawn I will insist that she be taken to a doctor, counsellor or psychiatrist for proper guidance and treatment.

context: 'What will you do?' — five situations, each to be answered with the action you would take. Q.4 carries an internal choice: the candidate answers any ONE of Q.4(i) or Q.4(ii).
stem: What will you do? You have to use free space around your home for good purpose.
solution: I will put the open space around my home to a socially and environmentally useful purpose. I will plant trees, flowering plants and a kitchen garden of vegetables and medicinal plants, and grow them with organic manure prepared from the wet waste of my house (composting/vermicomposting). I will make a rain-water harvesting pit or a soak pit there so that rain water is collected and the ground water is recharged, and I will keep separate bins for dry and wet waste. A part of the space can be kept clean and open as a play area for the children of the locality, with a bird bath and a nest box for birds. This makes the surroundings green, clean and healthy and helps conserve the environment.

context: 'What will you do?' — five situations, each to be answered with the action you would take. Q.4 carries an internal choice: the candidate answers any ONE of Q.4(i) or Q.4(ii).
stem: What will you do? Your brother studying in XII has developed the stress.
solution: Examination stress is common in Std XII, so I will help my brother manage it instead of ignoring it. I will talk to him, listen to his worries and assure him that marks are not the only measure of success. I will help him prepare a realistic study time-table with short breaks, so that study becomes regular and the burden is spread out. I will encourage him to sleep for seven to eight hours, eat a balanced diet, avoid excessive tea/coffee and mobile use, and to do exercise, yoga, pranayama and meditation daily, along with some recreation such as music, games or a walk. I will ask my parents not to compare him with others or put pressure of expectations on him, and if the stress continues I will suggest that he take the help of a teacher, counsellor or doctor.
